summary: Oil falls on hopes of a US-Iran deal after the midterms, Trump promises vetoes, Kyiv loses water, Israel's coalition race tilts, and climate and Ebola efforts move.

topics.heading: Oil falls 8.7% as the US vote raises hopes of an Iran deal; tankers burn near Hormuz
topics.summary: Brent crude fell 8.7% to $94.62 on Wednesday as traders bet that Trump, weakened by the midterms, will seek a deal with Iran.[^1] Iran's leaders said US voters rejected the war, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards say more tankers caught fire near the strait.[^2][^4]

lead.title: Oil slumps after midterm election rebuke to Trump raises bets on Iran war exit

alsoReported.title: Iranian leaders say midterm results show U.S. voters have rejected Trump's war
Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan 'unconvincing'; Trump confirms strikes

article: The price of Brent crude, the main global oil benchmark, fell $8.98, or 8.7%, to settle at $94.62 a barrel on Wednesday, its lowest close since August 31[^1]. It had been near $118 a week earlier, according to Gulf News[^5]. Reuters reports traders see a better chance that the war, which began on February 28, will end, because Tuesday's midterm defeat gives Trump more reason to seek a deal[^1][^2]. US stocks rose sharply the same day[^9].

Trump has said the war played a part in his party's losses, while also saying he would do it again[^1][^5]. Vice President JD Vance, who Axios reports is leading the advisers who want a deal, said "the reason we lost is the war"[^10][^5]. Qatar says both sides "remain committed" to talks and is passing proposals between them; it wants both to back a draft with three days of confidence-building steps that could restart direct talks[^3][^5].

Iran's leaders read the vote as a win. Chief negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf wrote that "Americans said NO TO WAR", but Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone expecting concessions is "gravely mistaken"[^2]. Iran says the strait reopens only if the US ends its naval blockade, lifts sanctions and releases frozen funds[^5][^3]. A senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides are still "far from a deal"[^1].

The strait itself is still dangerous. Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) say several tankers caught fire on Wednesday and Thursday after hitting mines or leaving the routes Iran allows; these claims have not been independently confirmed[^2][^4]. US officials told Axios the military is finishing preparations for a possible return to major combat, though "preparations are not an order"[^5].

Why it matters: oil prices feed into the cost of fuel, food and transport everywhere. NPR notes US gasoline averages $4.12 a gallon, about $1 more than a year ago, and analysts say pump prices could take months to fall even after a lasting deal[^10]. My read: markets are pricing in peace faster than diplomats are delivering it, so prices could swing again on any new strike.
topics.differences: Qatar says both sides are committed to talks; a senior Iranian official told Reuters they are far from a deal[^3][^1]. On Wednesday's tankers, Al Jazeera reports the IRGC saying four were destroyed, while AP reports Iranian state TV saying they caught fire[^3][^2].

topics.heading: Trump vows vetoes as Democrats plan investigations after winning Congress
topics.summary: A day after Democrats won both houses, Trump said he was "a little bit surprised" and promised to veto their agenda.[^6] Democrats named their priorities and planned investigations, while many House races were still being counted.[^7]

lead.title: Democratic Party gains US House majority in 2026 midterm elections

alsoReported.title: Trump says he was 'a little bit surprised' after Democrats' big win in midterms
2026 House midterm election results as Democrats capture majority with major wins

article: The day after the midterms, President Trump said he was "a little bit surprised" by the Democrats' wins and thought "we would do better"[^6]. He blamed some candidates and high gas prices linked to the Iran war[^6]. He also said Democrats are "in control, but they're really not" because of his veto, the president's power to reject a bill, which Congress can override only with two-thirds of both chambers. He said he would consider an immigration deal if it is "appropriate"[^6].

Final numbers are not in. ABC's tracker shows Democrats with 54 Senate seats, and CBS said early Wednesday that about 75 House races were still undecided[^6][^7]. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, likely the next Speaker, says he expects at least 255 Democratic seats out of 435[^7]. Several Republicans conceded close races during the day[^7].

Democrats have begun saying what they will do from January 3, when the new Congress sits[^8]. Jeffries lists reversing Medicaid and food-aid (SNAP) cuts, extending expired health-insurance tax credits, ending the Iran war and rolling back tariffs[^7]. Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, plans investigations into the Trump family's business dealings and immigration enforcement, among other things; the White House calls them "sham" probes[^7].

Markets took the result calmly. The Dow rose 3% on Wednesday, its best day since April last year, as investors welcomed predictability and falling oil prices[^9]. Exit polls put Trump's approval at 38%, according to CBS[^7].

What comes next: Republicans choose new House leaders, since Speaker Mike Johnson will not run for minority leader, and Friday brings the October jobs report[^7]. My read: with Trump holding the veto and Democrats holding the budget and investigations, the next two years look more likely to bring standoffs than big new laws.

topics.heading: Russian strikes cut Kyiv's water as Ukraine and its partners prepare for Abu Dhabi talks
topics.summary: A Russian attack on Ukraine's energy system caused Kyiv's worst water outage of the war, and a strike on an aid centre has killed at least 37.[^11][^14] Ukraine, the US and Europeans met in Brussels before talks with Russia on Nov 10-11.[^12]

lead.title: Russian strikes cause Kyiv's worst water outage of full-scale war

alsoReported.title: Ukraine, partners coordinate peace efforts ahead of Abu Dhabi talks with Russia
Russia says it hit Ukrainian postal hub and ship as Ukraine strikes Ryazan

article: Russia's November 3 attack on Ukraine's energy system, the largest this year, left Kyiv almost entirely without running water, according to the city's water utility; many residents went more than 24 hours without it before the system was stabilized on November 4[^11]. One water expert called it "the most serious water outage in Kyiv since the war began"[^11]. Ukraine says Russia launched 310 drones overnight into November 4 and that it shot down 272; energy sites in several regions were hit and emergency power cuts followed[^28].

In the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine's emergency service says 37 people, including two rescuers, were confirmed dead after a November 2 strike on a school used to hand out aid in Komyshuvakha, with dozens still missing[^14]. Ukraine keeps striking Russian oil refineries: the governor of Russia's Ryazan region says more than 200 Ukrainian drones attacked overnight, and verified footage showed a fire at the Ryazan refinery[^13].

Diplomacy continues alongside the fighting. On November 4 the European Commission hosted Ukraine, the US, Germany, France, the UK, NATO and the World Bank in Brussels to plan for Ukraine's post-war economy[^12]. The first three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are set for November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi, announced by US envoy Steve Witkoff[^25]. After a call with Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Zelenskyy said security guarantees "must be ironclad" and that air defence, especially Patriot interceptors, is a priority[^15].

Why it matters: attacks on power and water target civilians' ability to get through winter, and Ukraine's refinery strikes target Russia's oil income. Moscow still rejects a full ceasefire and demands that Ukraine give up the Donbas region[^12]. A ceasefire on energy and at sea, prisoner exchanges and the return of children taken to Russia are on the technical agenda for Abu Dhabi[^29]. My read: a limited deal on energy strikes is more realistic than a full peace soon.
topics.differences: Russia's Defence Ministry says it hit a postal terminal near Kharkiv and a cargo ship carrying military equipment off Odesa; Ukraine had not confirmed those strikes[^13].

topics.heading: Eisenkot wins more recommendations as Herzog weighs who forms Israel's next government
topics.summary: In talks with President Herzog, more parties backed Gadi Eisenkot than Benjamin Netanyahu to form a government, after the ultra-Orthodox UTJ declined to recommend anyone.[^16][^17] Herzog is due to choose a nominee within days.[^18]

lead.title: As Herzog consults party heads, Haredi faction says it won't recommend Netanyahu as PM

alsoReported.title: As Haredi allies withhold support for Netanyahu, Eisenkot poised to secure most endorsements
Israel's Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government

article: Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, met party leaders on November 4 and 5 to hear whom they recommend to form the next government after the October 27 election[^16][^17]. The certified results gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc 53 of the 120 seats, the Jewish opposition bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot 48, and Arab-led parties a record 19; a government needs 61[^18].

The biggest surprise came from United Torah Judaism (UTJ), an ultra-Orthodox alliance that has long backed Netanyahu. It recommended no one, and its Degel HaTorah faction said it acted on its rabbis' instructions[^16][^17]. Religious Zionism, Shas and Otzma Yehudit backed Netanyahu, while Yisrael Beytenu, The Democrats, Ra'am and others backed Eisenkot[^16][^17]. Ynet counts 56 seats behind Eisenkot and 46 behind Netanyahu; the Joint List, with 11 seats, had not yet announced its choice[^17].

Recommending someone is not the same as joining his government. Anadolu notes that if Ra'am and the Joint List both back Eisenkot he would reach 67 recommendations, but that would not mean they sit in his coalition[^26]. Whoever gets the mandate has 28 days, plus up to 14 more, to form a government; if both possible leaders fail, Israel could face another election early next year[^18][^16].

The elections committee found "no evidence of irregularities", rejecting claims from Netanyahu's camp that the vote was stolen[^18]. Herzog said, "The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality"[^18]. In Gaza, local officials said at least four people were killed in Israeli strikes on November 3; Israel says it struck militants[^27].

Why it matters: Israel's next government will shape what happens in Gaza's fragile truce and in the war with Iran. My read: Eisenkot looks likely to get the first chance, but turning recommendations from very different parties into a working coalition will be hard.
topics.differences: Counts differ by method. The Times of Israel and AP put Netanyahu's camp at 53, while Ynet gives 46 because it leaves out UTJ's seven seats, which went to no one[^16][^18][^17].

topics.heading: Brazil publishes a voluntary roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels ahead of COP31
topics.summary: Brazil, which led last year's UN climate summit, released a voluntary plan for countries to move away from coal, oil and gas, plus a plan to end deforestation by 2030.[^19] It will be discussed at COP31 in Türkiye, which opens Nov 9.[^19]

lead.title: 'The transition is inevitable': Brazil releases first global roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels

alsoReported.title: Brazil Releases Roadmaps to Phase Out Fossil Fuels, End Deforestation

article: On November 3, Brazil released what it calls a roadmap for phasing out coal, oil and gas, as the last act of its presidency of COP30, the UN climate summit held in Belém in 2025[^19]. It proposes three phases from 2028 to 2033 in which countries draft plans and change their energy systems, and says cuts in fossil-fuel production must "match declining demand"[^19][^20]. Brazil also published a roadmap to end deforestation by 2030[^19].

Background: at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, nearly 200 countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels, but the final COP30 deal did not mention them after opposition from some oil producers[^19]. Brazil's team says energy causes about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions and forest loss about 11%[^20]. The roadmap is voluntary; COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago said, "We are not suggesting negotiations… The agreements already exist"[^19].

Reactions are mixed. COP30 chief executive Ana Toni said "the transition is inevitable, so start planning now", while the campaign group 350.org warned the plan must not end up as a report "gathering dust"[^19]. The roadmap estimates that money for protecting forests needs to rise from $84.5 billion in 2023 to more than $300 billion a year by 2030[^20].

What comes next: COP31 runs November 9 to 20 in Antalya, Türkiye, with Australia leading the negotiations, and the roadmap is due for discussion on November 10[^19]. Euronews reports that a new fossil-fuel agreement there is considered unlikely[^19]. UN News notes that clean energy is growing fast, with electric vehicles about one in four new car sales in 2025, but developing economies outside China got only 18% of clean-energy investment[^24]. My read: the roadmap matters less as a rule than as a yardstick countries can be measured against.

topics.heading: WHO adds two vaccines made for the Bundibugyo Ebola strain to its Congo trial
topics.summary: Two experimental vaccines designed for the Bundibugyo Ebola virus will join a trial in Congo, the first such test during an outbreak of that strain.[^22] The outbreak has killed more than 5,300 people since May.[^21]

lead.title: WHO approves trials for two new Ebola vaccines

alsoReported.title: Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances

article: The World Health Organization said on November 4 that two new candidate vaccines will join a trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: one from the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and an mRNA vaccine from Moderna[^22]. It is the first time vaccines designed specifically against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola will be tested during an outbreak of it[^22].

The outbreak, which began in May, has killed more than 5,300 people, most of them in Congo, and Africa CDC reports 10,444 confirmed cases, making it the fastest-growing outbreak in the country's history[^21]. Kenya has reported nine cases and Nigeria one[^21]. The strain kills about half the people it infects, and until now no vaccine or treatment had been made for it; a trial that began last month uses Ervebo, a vaccine approved for a different strain[^21].

The trial uses ring vaccination: health workers vaccinate the contacts of each confirmed patient to build a protective ring around the case[^22]. It is led by Congo's national biomedical research institute with WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and Africa CDC, and funded by CEPI, a vaccine-research coalition[^22]. A separate trial is testing treatments, including antibody drugs and the antiviral remdesivir[^22].

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, "Vaccines alone will not end this outbreak, but they could become a powerful new tool"[^22]. He also urged countries to lift travel restrictions that he says "punish countries for doing the right thing"[^21]. Why it matters: an outbreak this large tests how fast the world can design, approve and deliver new vaccines, a lesson from COVID-19 now being tested again (my read).

topics.heading: Google faces backlash over tying Search in schools to its AI tools
topics.summary: Google said schools using its education software would lose Search unless they turned on its AI tools, then said after criticism that each can be switched on separately.[^23]

lead.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI

article: On November 3, Google announced that schools using its K-12 software, which millions of students use on Chromebooks, would lose access to Search unless they opted in to its AI tools[^23]. A Google education executive told the New York Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated"[^23]. After criticism, Google said Gemini, its Notebook tool and Search will each be off by default, and schools can turn them on separately[^23].

Many educators worry that AI-written answers at the top of search results will discourage students from working problems out for themselves[^23]. Critics went further: Senator Bernie Sanders called the plan "extortion", and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said no company should be able to "dictate how we teach our children"[^23]. Google says the change gives schools "more choice, not less" and that it is building a "Guided Learning" mode that walks students through problems instead of just giving answers[^23].

Background: US courts have found Google broke antitrust laws, the rules that limit how dominant companies use their power[^23]. AI companies are racing to get their tools into classrooms early, since students who learn on one system often keep using it; that is my judgment, not a reported fact.

Why it matters for you: Ontario schools also use Google tools, though this announcement was about US schools and the report does not mention Canada[^23]. My read: the deeper question is not whether AI is in school, but who decides how it is used: teachers, school boards, or the companies that make the software.

question.text: This week's reports of burning tankers near Hormuz come mostly from Iran's Revolutionary Guards and have not been independently confirmed. What would you need to see before treating such a claim as fact, and why might each side want you to believe its version?

read.summary: A clear guide to what nearly 200 countries will argue about at COP31 in Antalya from Nov 9: money, adaptation, emissions cuts, and why progress is both real and too slow.
